newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn vows to press ahead with tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Bonn vows to press ahead with tax reform.

text.p: Germany's government vowed on Friday to push through tax reforms even if it takes until the turn of the century, while the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) called for early elections to clear Bonn's political logjam.
A top aide to Chancellor Helmut Kohl said the government would not be deflected from its course even though the SPD had blocked its tax-cutting plan in parliament's reconciliation process this week.
"The tax reform will come. If not now, then at the latest by the year 2000," Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) told the Bild daily.

Schaeuble said the government would force a second meeting this autumn of parliament's mediation committee -- a body designed to break legislative deadlock between the two houses of parliament -- to keep up the pressure on the SPD.

"When people realise the SPD is blocking efforts to bring down unemployment just to make itself out as the 'saviour in an emergency' at the next election, then the SPD will very quickly be ready to agree," Schaueble told the newspaper.

But an opinion poll indicated the vast majority of voters thought both government and opposition were to blame for the failure of the tax reform plans. More people blamed the government than the SPD, the poll also found.
The representative survey for ARD television's Bericht aus Bonn programme found that 59 percent thought the opposing camps carried the repsonsibility together.
Only 12 percent thought the SPD should take all the blame and 19 percent thought the government was solely responsible.
The SPD said it would under no circumstances be persuaded to support Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to cut 30 billion marks ($16.2 billion) in income and corporate taxes.
The best solution, party leader Oskar Lafontaine said, would be for Kohl to bring the autumn 1998 national vote forward to spare Germany a 14-month election campaign.
"The tax chaos shows that the best solution now would be early elections," Lafontaine told the newspaper Saarbruecker Zeitung.
"But we must expect the ruling coalition to prolong this tragic play until September 1998 for fear of losing power."

Opinion polls show Lafontaine could secure control of both houses of parliament next year in coalition with the Green party. And, if the SPD wins the election, it would immediately introduce its own tax reforms, he said.
"Straight after the 1998 general election we would launch our own tax reform to lighten the burden on workers and families, and create a fairer and simpler tax system," he said.
Government spokesman Peter Hausmann said he was convinced that a second round of parliamentary mediation would increase the chances of a deal with the opposition.
"We see good chances of reaching a good result in a second mediation process," Hausmann told a news conference.

Restarting parliamentary mediation postpones an awkward decision for Kohl's centre-right coalition over whether to pass a separate bill to break out a cut in the solidarity income tax surcharge from the main tax reform.
Junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) have wrung a pledge out of the Christian Democrats to cut the 7.5 percent "soli" by two percentage points next year, and want that to be honoured.

"I am certain that we in the coalition can agree on a way to cut the burden on taxpayers as well as the soli, and maintain sound state finances," FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms told German Radio.

But, analysts say, the CDU fears that its eastern German wing could rebel against a cut in the soli -- raised to help rebuild the region's depressed economy -- and unite with the SPD to block a measure which would cost seven billion marks.

Schaeuble was non-committal on the solidarity surcharge: "We have agreed to cut the solidarity surcharge. We stand by this objective. But we must remember that we can only do what can be financed," he said. ($ = 1.846 German Marks)
